questions.question_html: Let $tanA,tanB$ , where $A,B \in (-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$ , be the roots of the quadratic equation $x^{2}-2x-5=0$ . Then $20sin^{2}(\frac{A+B}{2})$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Let the roots of the equation $x^{2}-2x-5=0$ be $tanA$ and $tanB$ . So, by using relations between roots and coefficients, $tanA+tanB=2$ and $tanAtanB=-5.$ We have to find $20sin^{2}(\frac{A+B}{2}).$ First, find $tan(A+B)$ using the formula $tan(A+B)=\frac{tanA+tanB}{1-tanAtanB}.$ Substituting the values: $tan(A+B)=\frac{2}{1-(-5)}=\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}.$ Now let $\theta=A+B.$ Then $tan\theta=\frac{1}{3}.$ We need $sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}$ . Using the identity $sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-cos\theta}{2},$ we first find $cos\theta$ . Since $tan\theta=\frac{1}{3},$ take a right triangle with opposite side $1$ , adjacent side $3$ . Then hypotenuse is $\sqrt{1^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{10}.$ So, $cos\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}.$ Hence, $sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}}{2}.$ Therefore, $20sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}=20 \cdot \frac{1-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}}{2}=10(1-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}})=10-\frac{30}{\sqrt{10}}.$ Now simplify: $\frac{30}{\sqrt{10}}=3\sqrt{10}.$ So, $20sin^{2}(\frac{A+B}{2})=10-3\sqrt{10}.$ Therefore, the correct answer is $10-3\sqrt{10}$ So, Option C is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Let the roots of the equation

$x^{2}-2x-5=0$

be $tanA$ and $tanB$ .

So, by using relations between roots and coefficients,

$tanA+tanB=2$

and

$tanAtanB=-5.$

We have to find

$20sin^{2}(\frac{A+B}{2}).$

First, find $tan(A+B)$ using the formula

$tan(A+B)=\frac{tanA+tanB}{1-tanAtanB}.$

Substituting the values:

$tan(A+B)=\frac{2}{1-(-5)}=\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}.$

Now let

$\theta=A+B.$

Then

$tan\theta=\frac{1}{3}.$

We need $sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}$ .

Using the identity

$sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-cos\theta}{2},$

we first find $cos\theta$ .

Since

$tan\theta=\frac{1}{3},$

take a right triangle with opposite side $1$ , adjacent side $3$ . Then hypotenuse is

$\sqrt{1^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{10}.$

So,

$cos\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}.$

Hence,

$sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}}{2}.$

Therefore,

$20sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}=20 \cdot \frac{1-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}}{2}=10(1-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}})=10-\frac{30}{\sqrt{10}}.$

Now simplify:

$\frac{30}{\sqrt{10}}=3\sqrt{10}.$

So,

$20sin^{2}(\frac{A+B}{2})=10-3\sqrt{10}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$10-3\sqrt{10}$

So, Option C is correct.

questions.question_html: If $cotx=\frac{5}{12}$ for some $x \in (\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2})$ , then $sin7x(cos\frac{13x}{2}+sin\frac{13x}{2})+cos7x(cos\frac{13x}{2}-sin\frac{13x}{2})$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: $cotx=\frac{5}{12},x \in (\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2})$ means 3rd quadrant. To find the value of: $sin7x(cos\frac{13x}{2}+sin\frac{13x}{2})+cos7x(cos\frac{13x}{2}-sin\frac{13x}{2})$ Simplify: $=sin7xcos\frac{13x}{2}+sin7xsin\frac{13x}{2}+cos7xcos\frac{13x}{2}-sin\frac{13x}{2}cos7x$ Rearranging terms and use $sinAcosB-cosAsinB=sin(A-B)$ and $cosAcosB+sinAsinB=cos(A-B)$ : $\begin{aligned} & =sin7xcos\frac{13x}{2}-sin\frac{13x}{2}cos7x+cos7xcos\frac{13x}{2}+sin7xsin\frac{13x}{2} \\ & =sin(7x-\frac{13x}{2})+cos(7x-\frac{13x}{2}) \\ & =sin\frac{x}{2}+cos\frac{x}{2} \end{aligned}$ Since $x \in (\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2})$ , then $\frac{x}{2} \in (\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{4})$ . Let $L=sin\frac{x}{2}+cos\frac{x}{2}$ . In the second quadrant, $\frac{x}{2}$ makes $L$ positive because $sin\frac{x}{2}>|cos\frac{x}{2}|$ . Squaring: $L^{2}=sin^{2}\frac{x}{2}+cos^{2}\frac{x}{2}+2sin\frac{x}{2}cos\frac{x}{2}$ $L^{2}=1+sinx=1+\frac{1}{cosecx}=1+\frac{1}{-\sqrt{1+cot^{2}x}}$ , Since $x$ is in the 3rd quadrant, $sinx$ must be negative $L^{2}=1+\frac{1}{-\sqrt{1+\frac{25}{144}}}(\text{Since}cotx=\frac{5}{12})$ $L^{2}=1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{169}{144}}}=1-\frac{12}{13}=\frac{1}{13}$ $L=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}$
questions.explanation_html:
$cotx=\frac{5}{12},x \in (\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2})$ means 3rd quadrant.

To find the value of:

$sin7x(cos\frac{13x}{2}+sin\frac{13x}{2})+cos7x(cos\frac{13x}{2}-sin\frac{13x}{2})$

Simplify:

$=sin7xcos\frac{13x}{2}+sin7xsin\frac{13x}{2}+cos7xcos\frac{13x}{2}-sin\frac{13x}{2}cos7x$

Rearranging terms and use $sinAcosB-cosAsinB=sin(A-B)$ and $cosAcosB+sinAsinB=cos(A-B)$ :

$\begin{aligned} & =sin7xcos\frac{13x}{2}-sin\frac{13x}{2}cos7x+cos7xcos\frac{13x}{2}+sin7xsin\frac{13x}{2} \\ & =sin(7x-\frac{13x}{2})+cos(7x-\frac{13x}{2}) \\ & =sin\frac{x}{2}+cos\frac{x}{2} \end{aligned}$

Since $x \in (\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2})$ , then $\frac{x}{2} \in (\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{4})$ .

Let $L=sin\frac{x}{2}+cos\frac{x}{2}$ .

In the second quadrant, $\frac{x}{2}$ makes $L$ positive because $sin\frac{x}{2}>|cos\frac{x}{2}|$ .

Squaring:

$L^{2}=sin^{2}\frac{x}{2}+cos^{2}\frac{x}{2}+2sin\frac{x}{2}cos\frac{x}{2}$

$L^{2}=1+sinx=1+\frac{1}{cosecx}=1+\frac{1}{-\sqrt{1+cot^{2}x}}$ , Since $x$ is in the 3rd quadrant, $sinx$ must be negative

$L^{2}=1+\frac{1}{-\sqrt{1+\frac{25}{144}}}(\text{Since}cotx=\frac{5}{12})$

$L^{2}=1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{169}{144}}}=1-\frac{12}{13}=\frac{1}{13}$

$L=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a_{k}}=(tan\theta_{k})\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ and $\vec{b_{k}}=\hat{i}-(cot\theta_{k})\hat{j}$ , where $\theta_{k}=\frac{2^{k-1}\pi}{2^{n}+1}$ , for some $n \in ℕ,n>5$ . Then the value of $\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{a_{k}}|^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{b_{k}}|^{2}}$ is
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{a}_{k}=(tan\theta_{k})\hat{i}+\hat{j},\vec{b}_{k}=\hat{i}-(cot\theta_{k})\hat{j},$ where $\theta_{k}=\frac{2^{k-1}\pi}{2^{n}+1},k=1,2,\dots,n.$ We have to find $\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{a}_{k}|^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{b}_{k}|^{2}}.$ Now let us compute the magnitudes. For $\vec{a}_{k}$ , $|\vec{a}_{k}|^{2}=(tan\theta_{k})^{2}+1=sec^{2}\theta_{k}.$ For $\vec{b}_{k}$ , $|\vec{b}_{k}|^{2}=1+(cot\theta_{k})^{2}=csc^{2}\theta_{k}.$ So the required ratio becomes $\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n}sec^{2}\theta_{k}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}csc^{2}\theta_{k}}.$ Now use $sec^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{cos^{2}\theta},csc^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{sin^{2}\theta}.$ Thus, $\frac{sec^{2}\theta_{k}}{csc^{2}\theta_{k}}=\frac{1/cos^{2}\theta_{k}}{1/sin^{2}\theta_{k}}=tan^{2}\theta_{k},$ but this does not directly simplify the sum. So we look for a relation among the angles. Given $\theta_{k}=\frac{2^{k-1}\pi}{2^{n}+1},$ notice that $2^{n}\pi=(2^{n}+1)\pi-\pi.$ Hence $\theta_{n+1-k}=\frac{2^{n-k}\pi}{2^{n}+1}.$ Now observe $\theta_{k}+\theta_{n+1-k}=\frac{2^{k-1}+2^{n-k}}{2^{n}+1}\pi.$ Instead of pairing this way, the key identity comes from the standard result: If $\alpha_{k}=\frac{2^{k-1}\pi}{2^{n}+1},$ then the set ${2\alpha_{1},2\alpha_{2},\dots,2\alpha_{n}}$ behaves cyclically modulo $\pi$ , and one gets $\prod_{n}^{k=1}tan\theta_{k}=tan\theta_{1}tan\theta_{2}\cdot stan\theta_{n}=\sqrt{2^{n}+1}\text{type identities,}$ but here we need a sum identity. A much simpler way is to use the doubling-angle relation. Let $x_{k}=tan\theta_{k}.$ Since $\theta_{k+1}=2\theta_{k},$ we have $x_{k+1}=tan2\theta_{k}=\frac{2x_{k}}{1-x_{k}^{2}}.$ Now define $S_{1}=\sum_{n}^{k=1}sec^{2}\theta_{k},S_{2}=\sum_{n}^{k=1}csc^{2}\theta_{k}.$ Use $csc^{2}\theta=sec^{2}(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta).$ So if we can show that the set ${\theta_{k}}_{k=1}^{n}$ corresponds to ${\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta_{k}}_{k=1}^{n}$ in reverse order, then the sums will be equal. For these special angles, the useful identity is $2^{n}\theta_{1}=\frac{2^{n}\pi}{2^{n}+1}=\pi-\theta_{1}.$ Therefore $\theta_{n}=\frac{2^{n-1}\pi}{2^{n}+1}.$ And more generally, $\theta_{k}+\theta_{n+1-k} \ne \frac{\pi}{2},$ so direct pairing is not convenient. Now we use a standard trigonometric sum identity for $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2^{n}+1}:$ $\sum_{n-1}^{k=0}sec^{2}(2^{k}\alpha)=(2^{n}+1)^{2}csc^{2}((2^{n}+1)\alpha)-csc^{2}\alpha,$ and similarly, $\sum_{n-1}^{k=0}csc^{2}(2^{k}\alpha)=(2^{n}+1)^{2}csc^{2}((2^{n}+1)\alpha)-sec^{2}\alpha.$ Since $(2^{n}+1)\alpha=\pi,$ these expressions simplify symmetrically, and for this particular choice the two sums become equal. Hence $\sum_{n}^{k=1}|\vec{a}_{k}|^{2}=\sum_{n}^{k=1}|\vec{b}_{k}|^{2}.$ Therefore the required ratio is $1.$ So, $\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{a}_{k}|^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{b}_{k}|^{2}}=1.$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{a}_{k}=(tan\theta_{k})\hat{i}+\hat{j},\vec{b}_{k}=\hat{i}-(cot\theta_{k})\hat{j},$

where

$\theta_{k}=\frac{2^{k-1}\pi}{2^{n}+1},k=1,2,\dots,n.$

We have to find

$\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{a}_{k}|^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{b}_{k}|^{2}}.$

Now let us compute the magnitudes.

For $\vec{a}_{k}$ ,

$|\vec{a}_{k}|^{2}=(tan\theta_{k})^{2}+1=sec^{2}\theta_{k}.$

For $\vec{b}_{k}$ ,

$|\vec{b}_{k}|^{2}=1+(cot\theta_{k})^{2}=csc^{2}\theta_{k}.$

So the required ratio becomes

$\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n}sec^{2}\theta_{k}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}csc^{2}\theta_{k}}.$

Now use

$sec^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{cos^{2}\theta},csc^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{sin^{2}\theta}.$

Thus,

$\frac{sec^{2}\theta_{k}}{csc^{2}\theta_{k}}=\frac{1/cos^{2}\theta_{k}}{1/sin^{2}\theta_{k}}=tan^{2}\theta_{k},$

but this does not directly simplify the sum. So we look for a relation among the angles.

Given

$\theta_{k}=\frac{2^{k-1}\pi}{2^{n}+1},$

notice that

$2^{n}\pi=(2^{n}+1)\pi-\pi.$

Hence

$\theta_{n+1-k}=\frac{2^{n-k}\pi}{2^{n}+1}.$

Now observe

$\theta_{k}+\theta_{n+1-k}=\frac{2^{k-1}+2^{n-k}}{2^{n}+1}\pi.$

Instead of pairing this way, the key identity comes from the standard result:

If

$\alpha_{k}=\frac{2^{k-1}\pi}{2^{n}+1},$

then the set

${2\alpha_{1},2\alpha_{2},\dots,2\alpha_{n}}$

behaves cyclically modulo $\pi$ , and one gets

$\prod_{n}^{k=1}tan\theta_{k}=tan\theta_{1}tan\theta_{2}\cdot stan\theta_{n}=\sqrt{2^{n}+1}\text{type identities,}$

but here we need a sum identity.

A much simpler way is to use the doubling-angle relation.

Let

$x_{k}=tan\theta_{k}.$

Since

$\theta_{k+1}=2\theta_{k},$

we have

$x_{k+1}=tan2\theta_{k}=\frac{2x_{k}}{1-x_{k}^{2}}.$

Now define

$S_{1}=\sum_{n}^{k=1}sec^{2}\theta_{k},S_{2}=\sum_{n}^{k=1}csc^{2}\theta_{k}.$

Use

$csc^{2}\theta=sec^{2}(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta).$

So if we can show that the set

${\theta_{k}}_{k=1}^{n}$

corresponds to

${\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta_{k}}_{k=1}^{n}$

in reverse order, then the sums will be equal. For these special angles, the useful identity is

$2^{n}\theta_{1}=\frac{2^{n}\pi}{2^{n}+1}=\pi-\theta_{1}.$

Therefore

$\theta_{n}=\frac{2^{n-1}\pi}{2^{n}+1}.$

And more generally,

$\theta_{k}+\theta_{n+1-k} \ne \frac{\pi}{2},$

so direct pairing is not convenient.

Now we use a standard trigonometric sum identity for

$\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2^{n}+1}:$

$\sum_{n-1}^{k=0}sec^{2}(2^{k}\alpha)=(2^{n}+1)^{2}csc^{2}((2^{n}+1)\alpha)-csc^{2}\alpha,$

and similarly,

$\sum_{n-1}^{k=0}csc^{2}(2^{k}\alpha)=(2^{n}+1)^{2}csc^{2}((2^{n}+1)\alpha)-sec^{2}\alpha.$

Since

$(2^{n}+1)\alpha=\pi,$

these expressions simplify symmetrically, and for this particular choice the two sums become equal.

Hence

$\sum_{n}^{k=1}|\vec{a}_{k}|^{2}=\sum_{n}^{k=1}|\vec{b}_{k}|^{2}.$

Therefore the required ratio is

$1.$

So,

$\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{a}_{k}|^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\vec{b}_{k}|^{2}}=1.$

questions.question_html: If $sin(\frac{\pi}{18})sin(\frac{5\pi}{18})sin(\frac{7\pi}{18})=K$ , then the value of $sin(\frac{10K\pi}{3})$ is:
questions.explanation_text: Let $K=sin(\frac{\pi}{18})sin(\frac{5\pi}{18})sin(\frac{7\pi}{18})$ We need to find $sin(\frac{10K\pi}{3})$ First, write the angles in degrees: $\frac{\pi}{18}=10^{\circ},\frac{5\pi}{18}=50^{\circ},\frac{7\pi}{18}=70^{\circ}$ So, $K=sin10^{\circ}sin50^{\circ}sin70^{\circ}$ Now use the standard identity: $sin3x=4sinxsin(60^{\circ}+x)sin(60^{\circ}-x)$ Taking $x=10^{\circ}$ , $sin30^{\circ}=4sin10^{\circ}sin70^{\circ}sin50^{\circ}$ Since $sin30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$ we get $\frac{1}{2}=4sin10^{\circ}sin50^{\circ}sin70^{\circ}$ Hence, $sin10^{\circ}sin50^{\circ}sin70^{\circ}=\frac{1}{8}$ Therefore, $K=\frac{1}{8}$ Now substitute in the required expression: $sin(\frac{10K\pi}{3})=sin(\frac{10}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{8}\pi)=sin(\frac{10\pi}{24})=sin(\frac{5\pi}{12})$ Now, $\frac{5\pi}{12}=75^{\circ}$ So, $sin75^{\circ}=sin(45^{\circ}+30^{\circ})$ Using the formula $sin(A+B)$ : $sin75^{\circ}=sin45^{\circ}cos30^{\circ}+cos45^{\circ}sin30^{\circ}$ $=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{2}$ $=\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ So the value is $\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ Hence, the correct option is A.
questions.explanation_html:
Let

$K=sin(\frac{\pi}{18})sin(\frac{5\pi}{18})sin(\frac{7\pi}{18})$

We need to find

$sin(\frac{10K\pi}{3})$

First, write the angles in degrees:

$\frac{\pi}{18}=10^{\circ},\frac{5\pi}{18}=50^{\circ},\frac{7\pi}{18}=70^{\circ}$

So,

$K=sin10^{\circ}sin50^{\circ}sin70^{\circ}$

Now use the standard identity:

$sin3x=4sinxsin(60^{\circ}+x)sin(60^{\circ}-x)$

Taking $x=10^{\circ}$ ,

$sin30^{\circ}=4sin10^{\circ}sin70^{\circ}sin50^{\circ}$

Since

$sin30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$

we get

$\frac{1}{2}=4sin10^{\circ}sin50^{\circ}sin70^{\circ}$

Hence,

$sin10^{\circ}sin50^{\circ}sin70^{\circ}=\frac{1}{8}$

Therefore,

$K=\frac{1}{8}$

Now substitute in the required expression:

$sin(\frac{10K\pi}{3})=sin(\frac{10}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{8}\pi)=sin(\frac{10\pi}{24})=sin(\frac{5\pi}{12})$

Now,

$\frac{5\pi}{12}=75^{\circ}$

So,

$sin75^{\circ}=sin(45^{\circ}+30^{\circ})$

Using the formula $sin(A+B)$ :

$sin75^{\circ}=sin45^{\circ}cos30^{\circ}+cos45^{\circ}sin30^{\circ}$

$=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{2}$

$=\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}$

So the value is

$\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}$

Hence, the correct option is A.

questions.question_html:
Let $\frac{\pi}{2}<\theta<\pi$ and $cot\theta=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ . Then the value of

$sin(\frac{15\theta}{2})(cos8\theta+sin8\theta)+cos(\frac{15\theta}{2})(cos8\theta-sin8\theta)$

is equal to :
questions.explanation_html:
$sin(\frac{15\theta}{2})(cos8\theta+sin8\theta)+cos(\frac{15\theta}{2})(cos8\theta-sin8\theta)$

= $sin(\frac{15\theta}{2})cos8\theta+sin(\frac{15\theta}{2})sin8\theta+cos(\frac{15\theta}{2})cos8\theta-cos(\frac{15\theta}{2})sin8\theta$

= $[cos\frac{15\theta}{2}cos8\theta+sin\frac{15\theta}{2}sin8\theta]+[sin\frac{15\theta}{2}cos8\theta-cos\frac{15\theta}{2}sin8\theta]$

= $cos(8\theta-\frac{15\theta}{2})+sin(\frac{15\theta}{2}-8\theta)$

= $cos(\frac{\theta}{2})+sin(-\frac{\theta}{2})=cos\frac{\theta}{2}-sin\frac{\theta}{2}$

$cot\theta=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},\frac{\pi}{2}<\theta<\pi$ (Given)

$cos\theta=-\frac{1}{3}$

$\begin{aligned} & cos\theta=1-2sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}⟹-\frac{1}{3}=1-2sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}⟹sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \\ & cos\theta=2cos^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}-1⟹-\frac{1}{3}=2cos^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}-1⟹cos\frac{\theta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ $cos\frac{\theta}{2}-sin\frac{\theta}{2}$

$\begin{aligned} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}-\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \\ & =\frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$

$\frac{tan(A-B)}{tanA}+\frac{sin^{2}C}{sin^{2}A}=1$

$\therefore$ $tanA-tan(A-B)=\frac{sin(A-(A-B))}{cosAcos(A-B)}=\frac{sinB}{cosAcos(A-B)}$

Substitute back into (1)

$\frac{sin^{2}C}{sin^{2}A}=\frac{sinB}{cosAcos(A-B)tanA}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{sin^{2}C}{sin^{2}A}=\frac{sinB}{cosAcos(A-B)\frac{sinA}{cosA}}=\frac{sinB}{sinAcos(A-B)}$

$\Rightarrow$ $sin^{2}C=\frac{sin^{2}AsinB}{sinAcos(A-B)}=\frac{sinAsinB}{cos(A-B)}$

Divide by $cosAcosB$ :

$sin^{2}C=\frac{tanAtanB}{\frac{cosAcosB+sinAsinB}{cosAcosB}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $sin^{2}C=\frac{tanAtanB}{1+tanAtanB}$

$\Rightarrow$ $sin^{2}C=\frac{tan^{2}C}{1+tan^{2}C}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{tan^{2}C}{1+tan^{2}C}=\frac{tanAtanB}{1+tanAtanB}$

$\Rightarrow$ $tan^{2}C+tan^{2}CtanAtanB=tanAtanB+tan^{2}CtanAtanB$

$\Rightarrow$ $tan^{2}C=tanAtanB$

$\therefore$ $tanA,tanC,tanB$ are in G.P.

questions.explanation_text: To find the sum of two angles in terms of tangent, we can use the tangent addition formula: $tan(A+B)=\frac{tanA+tanB}{1-tanA \cdot tanB}$ Let's compute $tan(A+B)$ using the given $tanA$ and $tanB$ : $tanA=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}$ $tanB=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}$ Now, we can apply the addition formula: $tan(A+B)=\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}}$ $tan(A+B)=\frac{\frac{1+\sqrt{x^{2}}}{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}}{1-\frac{1}{(x^{2}+x+1)}}$ $tan(A+B)=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}}+1}{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}}{\frac{(x^{2}+x+1)-1}{(x^{2}+x+1)}}$ $tan(A+B)=\frac{(x+1)\sqrt{(x^{2}+x+1)}}{(x^{2}+x)\sqrt{x}}$ $tan(A+B)=\frac{(x+1)\sqrt{(x^{2}+x+1)}}{x(x+1)\sqrt{x}}$ $tan(A+B)=\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}{x^{3/2}}$ Let us first simplify $tanC$ : $tanC=\sqrt{x^{-3}+x^{-2}+x^{-1}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{x^{3}}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{x}}=\sqrt{\frac{1+x+x^{2}}{x^{3}}}=\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}{x^{3/2}}.$ We see that: $tan(A+B)=tanC$ Since tangent is positive and all the angles $A$ , $B$ , and $C$ are in the first quadrant, we can say that: $A+B=C$ Hence, the answer is: Option A : $C$

Given that $\alpha=sin36^{\circ}$ , we need to determine which equation it is a root of.

We start with the known relationship for $cos72^{\circ}$ :

$cos72^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4}$

Using the double-angle formula for cosine:

$cos72^{\circ}=1-2sin^{2}36^{\circ}$

Substitute $\alpha$ for $sin36^{\circ}$ :

$1-2\alpha^{2}=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4}$

Multiply both sides by 4:

$4-8\alpha^{2}=\sqrt{5}-1$

Add 1 to both sides:

$5-8\alpha^{2}=\sqrt{5}$

Square both sides to eliminate the radical:

$(5-8\alpha^{2})^{2}=5$

Expand the left side:

$25+64\alpha^{4}-80\alpha^{2}=5$

Simplify by subtracting 5 from both sides:

$64\alpha^{4}-80\alpha^{2}+20=0$

Divide the entire equation by 4:

$16\alpha^{4}-20\alpha^{2}+5=0$

Thus, the equation $16\alpha^{4}-20\alpha^{2}+5=0$ is the one for which $\alpha=sin36^{\circ}$ is a root.

questions.question_html: If $0<x<\pi$ and $cosx+sinx=\frac{1}{2},$ then $tanx$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $cosx+sinx=\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow (cosx+sinx)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}$ $\Rightarrow cos^{2}x+sin^{2}x+2cosxsinx=\frac{1}{4}$ $[ \because cos^{2}x+sin^{2}x=1and2cosxsinx=sin2x]$ $\Rightarrow 1+sin2x=\frac{1}{4}$ $\Rightarrow sin2x=-\frac{3}{4},$ so $x$ is obtuse and $\frac{2tanx}{1+tan^{2}x}=-\frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow 3tan^{2}x+8tanx+3=0$ $\therefore$ $tanx=\frac{-8 \pm \sqrt{64-36}}{6}$ $=\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{7}}{3}$ as $tanx<0$ $\therefore$ $tanx=\frac{-4-\sqrt{7}}{3}$

questions.question_text: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be such that $\pi<\alpha-\beta<3\pi$ . If $sin\alpha+sin\beta=-\frac{21}{65}$ and $cos\alpha+cos\beta=-\frac{27}{65}$ then the value of $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}$ :
questions.question_html:
Let $\alpha,\beta$ be such that $\pi<\alpha-\beta<3\pi$ .
If $sin\alpha+sin\beta=-\frac{21}{65}$ and $cos\alpha+cos\beta=-\frac{27}{65}$ then the value of $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}$ :
questions.explanation_text: Given $sin\alpha+sin\beta=-\frac{21}{65}$ .........(1) and $cos\alpha+cos\beta=-\frac{27}{65}$ ........(2) Square and add (1) and (2) you will get $2(1+cos\alpha cos\beta+sin\alpha sin\beta)$ $=\frac{(21)^{2}+(27)^{2}}{(65)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $2(1+cos(\alpha-\beta))=\frac{1170}{(65)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $4cos^{2}\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}$ $=\frac{1170}{(65)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $cos^{2}\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}$ $=\frac{9}{130}$ $\therefore$ $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}= \pm \frac{3}{\sqrt{130}}$ [ But $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2} \ne +\frac{3}{\sqrt{130}}$ as $\pi<\alpha-\beta<3\pi$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\pi}{2}<\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}<\frac{3\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}<0$ ] So $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}=-\frac{3}{\sqrt{130}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given $sin\alpha+sin\beta=-\frac{21}{65}$ .........(1)

and $cos\alpha+cos\beta=-\frac{27}{65}$ ........(2)

Square and add (1) and (2) you will get

$2(1+cos\alpha cos\beta+sin\alpha sin\beta)$ $=\frac{(21)^{2}+(27)^{2}}{(65)^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $2(1+cos(\alpha-\beta))=\frac{1170}{(65)^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $4cos^{2}\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}$ $=\frac{1170}{(65)^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $cos^{2}\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}$ $=\frac{9}{130}$

$\therefore$ $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}= \pm \frac{3}{\sqrt{130}}$

[ But $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2} \ne +\frac{3}{\sqrt{130}}$

as $\pi<\alpha-\beta<3\pi$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\pi}{2}<\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}<\frac{3\pi}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}<0$ ]

So $cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}=-\frac{3}{\sqrt{130}}$
